old.name: Diani North — the river end
old.teaser: The strip fades into estuary, baobab and the 500-year-old mosque.
old.body: Where Diani began: the Mwachema mouth, the coral mosque, the Italian addresses around Colliers Centre, and the quietest hotel sand. The Kongo dugout leaves from here at sunset. Gombato side, north of Colliers Centre

old.name: Diani Central
old.teaser: Back-to-back hotels, bars and dive shops behind the whitest stretch of sand.
old.body: The postcard and the machinery in one: supermarkets, the cave restaurant, the beach clubs, the camel handlers, the tourist police post. Everything is walkable; nothing is far. If you stay one week with no car, stay here. Between the Ukunda junction turnoff and Nomad

q-galu.note: Galu + the southern strip; the forest patches are told in the green section: one clause

old.name: Galu
old.teaser: Administratively the sand changes name — and the pace drops by half.
old.body: Kinondo ward's beach: fewer walls, wider reef flat at low tide, the kite schools' home water, the fish landing at Mwaepe, and the deaf-staffed café on the sand. The strip's mellower second act. South of Nomad to Kinondo Kwetu country

old.name: Diani South & the forest patches
old.teaser: The canopy thickens and the monkeys cross overhead on rope.
old.body: South of the central cluster the Jadini forest remnants close over the road — this is colobridge country, with Colobus Conservation headquartered mid-stretch. Drive it slowly; the average is still 55 monkeys hit a year. Southern Diani Beach Road toward Galu

old.name: Ukunda town
old.teaser: The actual town: matatus, banks, markets, the airstrip — and the real food.
old.body: A workaday Swahili-Digo service centre on the highway. The mahamri mamas, the junction grills, the biryani rooms, the new covered market and the cheapest supermarket all live here, twenty minutes and one world from the sunbeds. Inland, at the A14 junction · Ukunda airstrip on the strip road

old.name: Tiwi
old.teaser: The quieter cousin: rough access roads, self-catering cottages, fishermen selling on the sand.
old.body: Across the Mwachema: low-key cottages, a campsite, and essentially no restaurant scene — villas self-cater and the fishermen sell direct. Wade over at low tide from the mosque, or drive round via the highway. The access roads are best not driven after dark, long-standing local advice. North of the Mwachema mouth

old.name: Tiwi, over the river
old.teaser: The quiet cousin — wade across at low tide from the mosque.
old.body: Not a drive at all if the tide cooperates: wade the Mwachema mouth from the Kongo Mosque and you are on Tiwi's near-empty sand. Twiga Lodge is the one documented kitchen (verify it is running); fishermen sell direct on the beach. Back before the flood. Access roads rough; not after dark — long-standing local advice

q-likoni.note: the arrival: ferry vs the bypass; the Mteza bridge fact lives in landmarks, one clause here

old.name: Likoni & Dongo Kundu — the arrival
old.teaser: The old ferry or the new bypass — since August 2024, finally a choice.
old.body: For decades the south coast began with the Likoni ferry queue — over 300,000 people a day at its peak. The Dongo Kundu bypass opened to the public in August 2024, its 1,440 m Mteza bridge the longest over water in the country, and made Diani a clean drive from Mombasa's airport. Untolled at last dated report (October 2025) — check before assuming. Arrival logistics live in the appendix below

q-kinondo.note: Chale Island resort has its own venue card and a dhow card: one clause

old.name: Kinondo
old.teaser: Rural Digo country behind the southernmost sand — home of the kaya.
old.body: The forest, the shrine, the quietest lodges and the health centre a Swedish hotel family built. Kaya Kinondo's visiting rules are the etiquette of the whole area: this is somebody's parish, behave accordingly. Behind Galu's southern end

old.name: Chale point & island
old.teaser: A private resort on the island's north half, a sacred grove on its south.
old.body: The mainland's tip faces the forested island 600 m out — resort by boat transfer only, kaya grove off-limits, and the new community mangrove boardwalk (April 2026) on the mainland shore. ~10 km south of the strip

old.name: Gazi
old.teaser: All nine Kenyan mangrove species and the project the world copies.
old.body: Mikoko Pamoja's home bay — carbon credits paying for wells and school books since 2010, an Equator Prize on the wall, and a women's boardwalk whose state you check locally. A working village, not a stop: buy the lunch, pay the guide. ~25 km south, off the A14

old.name: Msambweni
old.teaser: Fishing town, long lonely sand, thin visitor infrastructure — honestly.
old.body: The sub-county town south of the resort zone: a fishing economy, administrative offices, one whitewashed villa hotel and kilometres of beach with nobody on them. Go for the emptiness with your own arrangements; do not expect services. ~45 min south of the strip

q-shimoni-wasini.note: the place; the boat day lives in the dhow fold

old.name: Shimoni & Wasini
old.teaser: The dhow harbour and the car-free island — the full brief is in The dhow day.
old.body: Heavy history, working boats, the marine park's gateway. See The dhow day for the whole mechanism — crossing, caves, crab and all. ~75 min south · IBEAC's 1880s headquarters once stood here

old.name: Wasini Island
old.teaser: No roads, no cars — feet and wheelbarrows on coral lanes.
old.body: Around 3,000 people in fishing villages, an old Wa-vumba settlement built in and around its own ruins — a pillar tomb still holds its inset Chinese porcelain. Power arrived as a solar mini-grid in 2023. The crab lunch, the boardwalk and the paths are the island hour of the dhow day. 3 km crossing from Shimoni

old.name: Sunrise on the strip
old.teaser: The emptiest, best hour of the resort day — and the fishermen are already out.
old.body: Four degrees south of the equator the sun keeps office hours: up around 06:15, year-round. The beach before seven belongs to the monitors of the turtle programme, the ngalawa crews pushing out, and you. Walk north toward the river or south toward Galu; the askaris posted along the hotel frontages are your landmark chain. Whole strip · walkable at any tide on the upper beach

w-river-mouth.note: the walk; the mosque's story lives in culture (one clause)

old.name: Kongo Mosque & the river mouth
old.teaser: Baobabs, an estuary you can wade, and a coral mosque still in use after five centuries.
old.body: At the strip's north end the Mwachema river — locally the Kongo — meets the sea under giant baobabs beside the coral-rag Kongo Mosque, Diani's last surviving relic of the old Swahili settlements and one of a tiny handful of ancient coral mosques still in use in Kenya. At low tide you can wade the mouth across to Tiwi. It is a living mosque and its custodians keep rules on the adjacent sand: dress on the beach, no bottles, respect at prayer times. The madafu sellers here are the classic ones. Diani north / Gombato · time to the ebb · full story in Culture

w-reef-flat.note: one home for the reef-flat walk; Chale flats as the spring-low variant

old.name: The reef-flat walk
old.teaser: The lagoon empties and hands you the seabed — the full brief is in The Reef.
old.body: The signature walk of this coast, twice a month: central Diani to Galu over the drained lagoon at spring low. Urchins, tide pools, working fishers, and the water coming back on its own schedule — the safety and tide mechanics are in The reef, the wind & the sky . Diani central–Galu · 1.5–2.5 h · start on the ebb

old.name: The reef-flat walk
old.teaser: Central Diani to Galu over seagrass, tide pools and sandbars — 1.5–2.5 hours of seabed.
old.body: At spring low (new and full moon) the lagoon literally empties, leaving water only in the deeper channels. Walk out over the flats among the tide pools and the fishers working their lines and traps — this is the working end of a fishery that has fed the shore for centuries. The safety honesty: sea urchins are real and plentiful, stonefish exist, and the tide comes back without consulting you. Reef shoes always, an eye on the water line, and start on the ebb, not the flood. Whole strip; widest flats Diani central–Galu · check the tide table, go on the ebb

old.name: Chale point flats at spring low
old.teaser: The southern tip's version: exposed flats with the sacred island in view.
old.body: At big spring lows the flats between the mainland point and Chale Island partially expose — same lagoon mechanics as the whole coast, with the kaya grove across the channel for company. Watch the flood; the channel fills first. Chale point, past Kinondo · pair with the new community boardwalk

w-ukunda.note: do not name Ibiza Market as a pick (cut); the new covered market has its own card

old.name: Ukunda market & town walk
old.teaser: The junction, the stages, the kanga shops, the lunch kibandas — the strip's engine room.
old.body: From the matatu stage through the Ibiza market cluster and the new Mvindeni covered market: produce, tailors, spice stalls, mahamri smoke at dawn. Go with small notes and no flashing valuables; go guided (the Kaaribu tour, USD 25) if you want the doors opened and the mnazi den included. Ukunda town · mornings before the heat

w-gazi.note: the walk; Mikoko Pamoja's carbon story lives in the green section

old.name: Gazi Bay mangrove edge
old.teaser: The village shore of the world's most-studied mangrove bay.
old.body: Walk the shore of the bay that holds all nine Kenyan mangrove species and the Mikoko Pamoja project — combine with the women's boardwalk (confirm its state locally) and a village lunch. The science station has made this modest village a name in journals worldwide. Gazi, ~25 km south · morning tides

old.name: Shimoni history walk
old.teaser: The caves, the 1885 colonial ruins, the jetty and the channel.
old.body: The old dhow harbour walks in an hour or two: the slave caves (guided, community-run), the ruins of the Imperial British East Africa Company's 1880s headquarters, the working jetty and the channel views to Wasini. Heavy and worth it — the full cave brief is in The dhow day . Shimoni, ~75 min south · before or after the crossing

old.name: Pilli Pipa Dhow Safari
old.teaser: The institution: marine-biologist owners, two jahazis, every fee folded in.
old.body: Running since 1989 under owners who are marine biologists and dive instructors. The published day: two dedicated snorkel stops — Inner Kisite's sloping hard-coral wall among them — then its own Wasini lunch of coconut vegetable soup, crab claws, cassava bites and cardamom-clove rice. USD 137 adult / 66 child covers transfers, the KWS fees, kit and lunch (obs. 2026-08); scuba add-ons USD 40–70. Book days ahead in season. Office: Colliers Centre, Diani Beach Road · daily 07:00–17:00 · +254 724 442 555

d-charlie.note: the boat day; the crab lunch is in the venue card

old.name: Charlie Claw's dhows
old.teaser: The island house's own jahazis, with a twelve-point dolphin code.
old.body: The Wasini Island Restaurant runs its own large dhows to Kisite with PADI/BSAC diving and a published dolphin code of conduct: approach slow and parallel, twenty minutes maximum with the animals, never swim with, feed or touch them. Its community arm pays teachers' salaries in Shimoni, Wasini and Mkwiro. No public tariff — agree the package in writing; most Diani hotels book it. Booking +254 722 205 154 · Wasini Island · lunch peaks ~13:00 with the tour waves

old.name: Shimoni jetty, DIY
old.teaser: Local captains assemble the same day for less — you carry the checklist.
old.body: Local boat co-ops off the jetty run the Kisite circuit and a village lunch for a fraction of the packaged price — mostly motorised fibreglass rather than sail. Reports put locally-arranged packages around KES 3,000–4,500 a head plus park fees and boat share, but nothing is published or guaranteed: agree price, life jackets, snorkel kit, lunch and KWS fees before boarding, and be at the jetty by 08:30 with the tide. Shimoni jetty · mornings · cash · quality varies boat to boat

old.name: Kisite-Mpunguti Marine Park
old.teaser: 39 km² of coral islets at the Tanzania border — three resident dolphin species.
old.body: Gazetted 1978: bottlenose dolphins year-round on the reefs, humpback dolphins in the channel, spinner pods of 50–200. Humpback whales pass July–October, peak August. Official fees current for 2026: non-resident USD 25 adult / 15 child (East African KES 500, Kenya resident KES 675) plus a KES 1,000 dhow-excursion levy — reputable operators fold all of it in. Parks are cashless and single-use-plastic-free. Honest note: in December–January many boats converge on the same reefs mid-morning. KWS toll-free 0800 597 000 · Oct–Mar for 20 m+ visibility · Jun–Aug kusi chop drops it

old.name: Wasini women's coral boardwalk
old.teaser: 500 m of walkway over fossil coral, run by the island's 70-woman collective.
old.body: A looped boardwalk over fossilised coral heads and mangrove at the village edge — at high tide the sea floods in beneath the dead coral, which is the stranger, prettier sight. Built with KWS and villagers, operated by the Wasini Women Group; fees fund village welfare. Give it the half hour after lunch. Planks are weathered in stretches: flip-flops fine, heels absurd. Wasini village · daylight · KES 200 reported, unverified — pay what is asked

old.name: Wasini island paths
old.teaser: Car-free coral lanes between fishing villages — wheelbarrows are the traffic.
old.body: Cross from Shimoni and walk the sandy lanes and hardened coral trails between the villages — no roads, no cars, solar mini-grid power only since 2023. The women's coral boardwalk closes the loop, and the old pillar tomb with its inset Chinese porcelain states the island's trading past in one object. Wasini Island · with the dhow day, after lunch

old.name: Robinson Island sandbank
old.teaser: A sandbank that exists only at low tide — white sand, turquoise on all sides, nothing else.
old.body: Off the Gazi stretch, listed by the booking platforms as literally 'temporary sandbank': glass-bottom boats run short picnic trips timed to the ebb. Spring lows (new and full moon) raise the biggest bank. It disappears — a mistimed trip is a boat ride to open water — and there is zero shade and zero anything: pack water, and no single-use plastic in protected waters. Any beach-boat operator or hotel desk, day before · confirm the tide time yourself

old.name: Chale Island
old.teaser: A private-island resort sharing 31 acres with a sacred kaya grove and Kenya's only overwater bar.
old.body: Six hundred metres offshore: the north half is the renovated resort (sister of Nomad, seven restaurants and bars), the south half sacred Digo kaya that stays unbuilt. The sundowner at the overwater bar is the island's hour. Day access is the honest unknown — visitors report day passes, the resort publishes nothing, and the island itself has been in a land-recovery suit since 2021. Phone +254 709 538 880 before driving down; access is by resort boat across the tidal channel. Off Kinondo/Chale point · tide-dependent transfer · no independent arrival

old.name: The Kongo River dugout
old.teaser: The sundowner that isn't a bar: mangroves, birdlife, the 500-year-old mosque at the mouth.
old.body: Coral Spirit has run Diani's northern river for ten years: guided sunset canoe cruises through the Mwachema mangroves — birdlife, an old cave passage, the coral-rag Kongo Mosque at the mouth — plus SUP on the same flat water and a bonfire BBQ add-on on the beach. The web store shows everything 'sold out'; in practice you book by phone or WhatsApp a day ahead. After rains the river runs murky — that is the season, not a fault. Diani north / Gombato · +254 716 440 223 · last two hours of light, rising tide

old.name: Kaya Kinondo
old.teaser: The only sacred Mijikenda kaya open to visitors — kaniki wrap, Digo guide, no exceptions.
old.body: Thirty hectares of coral-rag forest sacred to the Digo, a UNESCO World Heritage component (2008) and national monument since 1992. In 2001 the elders offered a sacrifice to the ancestors and opened it to controlled visits — Kenya's first kaya ecotourism project. How it works: you wrap the provided black kaniki over your clothes, remove headwear, and walk with a Digo guide past the Chidzumba Cha Mwana Mlungu prayer hut, the medicinal trees, the 'hugging tree'. The etiquette is absolute: stay on the path, take nothing — not a leaf — no smoking, no alcohol, no public affection; photography restricted, ask first. Fees are opaque (reports run KES 1,000–2,000 for tours, obs. 2025-10; operator packages with transfer KES 6,000) — agree clearly before starting; M-Pesa or cash on arrival. A bookable all-female Digo dance troupe with kayamba rhythms performs after the walk; proceeds fund conservation, schools and the village. Kinondo, behind the southern strip · WhatsApp +254 745 797 653 · morning or from 15:00 — midday under the canopy edge is brutal

old.name: The kaya system, honestly
old.teaser: More kayas line this very road — and they are not attractions.
old.body: The UNESCO property inscribes ten forest sites along some 200 km of coast — remains of fortified Mijikenda villages, created from the sixteenth century, abandoned as villages by the 1940s, kept since as the abodes of ancestors. The National Museums have identified dozens more makaya beyond the inscribed ten, and guidebooks place kayas along the Diani road itself near the golf course and Diani Sea Lodge. They are closed, and that is the point: Kaya Kinondo is the single sanctioned door, opened by the elders on their terms. Respect the rest as you would a locked church. Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests · UNESCO ref 1231rev · inscribed 2008

old.name: Colobus Conservation
old.teaser: The eco-tour behind the colobridges — 500 primate rescues a year.
old.body: Founded 1997 out of community alarm at road deaths of the Angolan black-and-white colobus (IUCN Vulnerable). The famous colobridges — 29 rope ladders over Diani Beach Road, four more over private drives — cross the nine-kilometre cut where cars still hit an average of 55 monkeys a year. The guided eco-tour (45–60 minutes) walks the rescue and rehabilitation enclosures; the 24-hour rescue line handles some 500 primates in distress annually. Tour fee unpublished — expect cashless payment on arrival; the money strings the next bridge. No handling, ever: a working rescue facility, not a petting zoo. Diani Beach Road, southern strip · 24 h rescue line +254 711 479 453 · mornings, when the troops move

old.name: The colobridges
old.teaser: Rope ladders over the traffic — community engineering you can watch working.
old.body: Strung since 1997 over the nine-kilometre cut of 1971. Look up anywhere on the southern strip and eventually a troop crosses hand over hand above the matatus. The full story is in the green section ; the habit it should give you is a slow foot on the beach road. Diani Beach Road, densest toward the south

old.name: The Jadini forest patches
old.teaser: The last coastal hardwood of the strip — named after a hotel, kept by monkeys.
old.body: The surviving patches of coastal hardwood toward the strip's south end still carry the name of the Jadini hotel — more correctly the Diani Forest, alive with birds, butterflies, vervets and colobus, and losing ground every year. You do not visit it so much as notice it: the canopy over the road, the rope bridges, the troops at dawn on the powerlines. Drive the strip slowly forever after. Southern Diani Beach Road, around Colobus Conservation

old.name: Diani Turtle Watch
old.teaser: Fourteen monitors, fifty kilometres, and sometimes a dawn hatchling release.
old.body: Since 2012, Diani's community turtle programme: morning patrols along the whole south coast, at-risk nests relocated to accredited hatchery points on hotel beachfronts (hatchlings emerge 55–75 days later), strandings answered, necropsies run — which keep finding plastic. Over 441 hatchlings from sponsored nests by January 2025. There is no ticket desk and no promise: follow @dianiturtlewatch, tell your hotel's beach team you want the call, and if a release is announced while you are here, drop everything. Beach-wide programme, no premises · releases dawn/dusk, day-of notice

k-mikoko.note: one home for the mangrove carbon story

old.name: Mikoko Pamoja, Gazi Bay
old.teaser: The world's first community blue-carbon project — mangrove credits paying for village wells.
old.body: Launched 2010, Plan Vivo-certified, UN Equator Prize 2017: Gazi's community co-manages 117 hectares of mangroves, replants some 8,000 trees a year and has spent the carbon money on clean water for 3,500 people and books for 700 children. 'Mangroves together', literally. Visits are arranged through the project, often combined with the village women's boardwalk (a 200 m recycled-plastic rebuild whose current state you should confirm locally) and a Gazi lunch. Its newest sibling: the Chale Community Boardwalk at Kinondo, opened April 2026 — 100 metres into the mangroves, community-run, still raw. Gazi village, ~25 km south · morning low-to-rising tide · arrange via mikokopamoja.org

old.name: Gazi & the mangrove science
old.teaser: The Equator-Prize village: Mikoko Pamoja, the boardwalk, a village lunch.
old.body: The world's first community blue-carbon project and the bay every mangrove scientist knows. Arrange via the project, check the boardwalk's state locally, pay the guide fairly. Brief in the green section . Morning tides · combine with Msambweni's empty sand

old.name: Kongo Mosque
old.teaser: A coral mosque centuries old at the river mouth — dating disputed, use undisputed.
old.body: At the Mwachema mouth under the baobabs stands Diani's last surviving relic of the old Swahili settlements. The dating is honestly contested — the heritage inventory gives 14th–15th century; local tradition and press say 16th and even older — and the name, by the deputy imam's account, comes from a grave inscription 'Siddiq Kongo' found at the site; tradition holds it was abandoned when the Arab traders left and rediscovered some three centuries ago. What is undisputed: it is alive — hundreds at Friday prayers, thousands spilling onto the beach at Eid, a recent renovation that kept the ancient shell. Etiquette: dress properly on the adjacent sand (its custodians ban alcohol and nudity on that stretch), ask before entering outside prayer times, and treat the graves as graves. Diani north, river mouth · pair with the estuary walk and the madafu sellers

old.name: Kongo Mosque
old.teaser: Centuries of coral masonry, still praying — the strip's oldest working building.
old.body: The full brief is in Culture ; as a landmark it is the north end of everything — the estuary, the baobabs, the wade to Tiwi, the madafu trade, the sunset dugouts. Mwachema mouth, Diani north

c-shimoni-caves.note: one home for the caves: the visit and the shrine

old.name: The Shimoni caves & the shrine
old.teaser: Slave pen, then and before it a kaya shrine — both histories are true at once.
old.body: The full visiting brief is in The dhow day ; the cultural point belongs here. The caves were sacred to Digo elders before the slave trade used them, and one chamber is still a working shrine — red, white and black cloths, rosewater, incense; the guides explain the colours. That double history — shrine, atrocity, shrine again — is the south coast's memory in one room of coral. Shimoni · proceeds pay teachers and dispensary medicine

old.name: Shimoni slave caves
old.teaser: The shackles are still fixed in the coral. Go with the guide; let it be heavy.
old.body: In the 18th and early 19th centuries these coral chambers held enslaved people awaiting the dhows to Zanzibar and Pemba's markets — iron shackles and chain studs remain in the rock, per National Museums of Kenya curators. Before and after that history the caves were sacred, and one chamber is still a working shrine with ribbons, rosewater and incense. Community-run with NMK assistance; proceeds pay teachers and dispensary medicine. Bats, slippery coral steps, a history told plainly — a twenty-minute visit that outweighs the rest of the day. Steps from Shimoni jetty · two daily guided sessions reported · no verified fee to print — carry small cash

old.name: The Wasini pillar tomb
old.teaser: Chinese porcelain set into a Swahili tomb — the Indian Ocean trade in one object.
old.body: Wasini's old Wa-vumba settlement is built in and around its own ruins, and the pillar tomb still holding its inset Chinese porcelain says everything about what moved on the monsoon: goods, people, taste. Thirty seconds off the village path on the island hour. Wasini village · with the dhow day

old.name: The Galu baobab
old.teaser: The traditional end of Diani Beach is a tree.
old.body: Diani's core runs from the Kongo river to Galu, and the traditional southern marker is an old baobab — a boundary drawn in botany rather than surveying. Baobabs punctuate the whole strip (the 41's bar is built around one; giants frame the mosque); they are protected in practice by reverence, which on this coast is older than law. Galu beach · the neighbouring kayas explain the reverence

old.name: Ukunda airstrip
old.teaser: A 1,174 m tarmac runway between the beach and the highway — the coast's side door.
old.body: KAA-owned, unofficially 'Diani Airport': Safarilink and Jambojet connect it daily (Jambojet: about an hour from Nairobi), which is why a Diani week no longer starts with the ferry. The skydivers' Caravans use it too — the beach landings you see are briefed in the water section . Diani Beach Road, Ukunda · arrival brief in the appendix

old.name: The Two Fishes ruin
old.teaser: One of the ten majors of the 80s, now a lived-in ruin — the strip's memento mori.
old.body: The Two Fishes hotel — German-founded, once among Diani's ten — did not survive the contraction; its shell is now inhabited and worked around by local families, notable enough as a condition to carry its own academic paper on 'the politics of skeletons and ruination'. It is not a sight to visit — people live there — but knowing it is there recalibrates every brochure superlative on the strip. Southern strip · respect: homes, not a photo stop

old.name: The Mteza bridge
old.teaser: The longest bridge over water in Kenya — the reason your transfer no longer queues for a ferry.
old.body: The centrepiece of the Dongo Kundu bypass, opened August 2024, ending the Likoni ferry's monopoly on the south coast — a crossing that once moved over 300,000 people a day. Untolled at last dated report (Oct 2025); check before assuming. On the Mombasa approach · you will cross it without noticing, which is the point
